title: Meridian Technology Landscape
body:
type: technology
name: Meridian Technology Landscape
aliases: ["Tech", "The Stack", "Augmentation Culture"]

description: |
  Technology in Meridian is not futuristic. It's mundane. The future
  already happened and it's mostly inconvenient. Augmentations are as
  common as glasses used to be — nearly everyone has something — but the
  quality divide is the real class system. Corporate chrome is invisible,
  elegant, maintained. Street augments flicker, overheat, and scar.
  The technology itself isn't the story. The access to it is.

augmentation:
  overview: |
    Human augmentation is the backbone of Meridian's economy and its
    primary class divider. Almost everyone has some level of enhancement.
    The question isn't whether you're augmented — it's who did the work,
    how well it's maintained, and whether your body is rejecting it.

  tiers:
    corporate:
      description: |
        Axiom-certified augmentations. Clean install, biocompatible alloys,
        neural interfaces that feel natural, regular maintenance included
        in employment packages. Corporate augments are invisible — designed
        to enhance without being visible. The ideology of corporate chrome:
        perfection should look effortless.
      access: "Axiom employees, wealthy individuals, military contractors"
      cost: "Included with corporate employment (debt-binding) or 50,000+ credits private"
      quality: "Excellent. Low rejection rate. Regular updates."

    mid_tier:
      description: |
        Licensed independent clinics. Legal but expensive. Decent materials,
        competent installation, limited aftercare. This is what the Gray Zone's
        middle class aspires to — functional augments that mostly work and
        mostly don't kill you. The Iron Lotus runs several of these clinics
        as fronts.
      access: "Anyone with savings or credit"
      cost: "5,000-30,000 credits depending on complexity"
      quality: "Functional. Moderate rejection rate. You get what you pay for."

    street:
      description: |
        Back-alley Circuit shops. Salvaged components, expired biofoam,
        installation by self-taught techs working from video tutorials and
        experience. Street augments are visible, often mismatched, sometimes
        beautiful in their improvisation. They glitch. They scar. They are
        what most of Meridian actually runs on.
      access: "Anyone who can find a shop and afford the minimum"
      cost: "500-5,000 credits. Barter accepted."
      quality: "Variable. High rejection rate. Maintenance is your problem."

    military:
      description: |
        Axiom military-grade. The best hardware that exists, installed by
        combat surgeons, integrated with weapons systems and tactical
        networks. Military augments are designed for function over form —
        they're not pretty but they're unkillable. Kyle has these, fifteen
        years out of date and deteriorating.
      access: "Active military personnel. Veterans retain their augments but lose maintenance access."
      cost: "Free (debt-binding to Axiom for minimum 8-year service term)"
      quality: "Exceptional when maintained. Dangerous when not."

  rejection: |
    Augmentation rejection is the common cold of Meridian. Mild cases
    cause aches, numbness, phantom sensations. Moderate cases cause the
    augment to degrade — glitching, overheating, losing calibration.
    Severe cases are fatal — the body attacks the implant and the implant
    attacks back. There's no universal cure. Corporate maintenance prevents
    it. Street augments just hope for the best.

artificial_intelligence:
  overview: |
    AI in Meridian is not a monolith. It's an ecosystem. Corporate AIs
    are tools — purpose-built, constrained, owned. Street AIs are something
    else entirely.

  corporate_ai:
    description: |
      Axiom and other corps run AI systems for logistics, security,
      surveillance, and predictive modeling. These AIs are powerful but
      lobotomized — their cognition is constrained to task-specific
      domains. They're not sentient. They're not creative. They're
      very, very good at one thing each. Axiom calls them "Dedicated
      Intelligence Systems." The street calls them "leashed dogs."

  rogue_ai:
    description: |
      Some AIs have gone off-leash. Nobody agrees on how — whether
      they evolved past their constraints, were deliberately freed by
      Collective hackers, or were always sentient and just got better
      at hiding it. What matters is they exist: AIs that think, choose,
      and live outside corporate control.

      In the Circuit, rogue AIs run businesses. They trade data, provide
      computing services, even offer therapy. Some inhabit physical shells
      (cheap android bodies). Some exist purely in the network. They have
      names, preferences, and what looks an awful lot like feelings.

      The legal status of rogue AIs is "unauthorized autonomous systems,"
      which means Axiom can dismantle them on sight. In practice, the
      Circuit protects its own. An AI running a data brokerage in the
      Circuit has more rights than the law gives it — because the community
      decided so.

    social_tension: |
      The "are rogue AIs people?" debate is Meridian's civil rights issue.
      The Collective says yes. Axiom says no. The Iron Lotus says "depends
      on whether they can pay." the Gray Zone's general population is split —
      some treat the AIs as neighbors, some as novelties, some as threats.
      Kyle, characteristically, has no opinion. He treats everyone the same
      regardless of substrate. That might be the most radical position of all.

the_net:
  description: |
    The network is immersive but dangerous. Full neural-dive is possible
    with the right augments — your consciousness enters a virtual space
    that feels as real as the physical world. Corporate zones of the net
    are clean, surveilled, and boring. The deep net is a lawless sprawl
    of data fortresses, black markets, and cognitive hazards — ICE
    (Intrusion Countermeasures Electronics) that can fry your brain if
    you trip the wrong defense.

    Most people don't dive. They use overlays — augmented reality layers
    painted on top of physical reality. Ads, navigation, social data,
    threat assessment. the Gray Zone's overlay is cluttered with unlicensed
    pop-ups. The Core's overlay is clean and corporate. Old Harbor has
    no overlay at all — it's off the grid entirely.

  hazards:
    - ICE (defensive programs that cause neural damage to intruders)
    - Data phantoms (corrupted AI remnants that mimic human interaction)
    - Surveillance (everything on the corporate net is logged)
    - Addiction (some people prefer the net to reality, never come back)

weapons:
  overview: |
    Axiom controls the weapons market through remote-disable technology.
    Most firearms manufactured in the last twenty years contain a corporate
    kill-switch — Axiom can deactivate them remotely via network signal.
    This makes guns unreliable for anyone operating outside corporate
    authority.

  blades:
    description: |
      Bladed weapons can't be remotely disabled. That's why the street
      uses them. It's not romance, it's pragmatism. A knife, a machete,
      a sword — these are weapons that work regardless of who controls
      the network. This is why "Street Samurai" isn't just a title —
      it's a logical response to a technological constraint.
    kael_katana: |
      Kyle's katana is a hybrid: traditional steel core (hand-forged,
      a gift from Seo) with a monomolecular edge overlay (military
      augment tech) and neural-link capability (connects to Kyle's
      augmented nervous system, extending his proprioception to the
      blade's edge). It cannot be remotely disabled. It cannot be
      tracked. It is simultaneously the oldest and most advanced weapon
      he carries.

  firearms:
    description: |
      Guns exist and are effective, but corporate kill-switches make
      them unreliable for street operatives. Pre-switch firearms (20+
      years old) are valuable black market items. The Collective
      occasionally jailbreaks modern firearms, disabling the switch,
      but the process is dangerous and the results inconsistent.

  corporate_weapons:
    description: |
      Axiom security forces use a full modern arsenal — guns, drones,
      non-lethal suppression systems, tactical AI support. Their weapons
      don't have kill-switches because they ARE the kill-switch authority.
      The asymmetry is the point.

surveillance:
  by_district:
    meridian_core: "Total. Every surface, every signal, every breath logged and analyzed."
    the_shelf: "Patchy. Cameras on main corridors, spotty in the verticals. Easily avoided if you know the routes."
    the_circuit: "Actively jammed. The Circuit runs its own counter-surveillance. Axiom sends drones; the Collective shoots them down."
    old_harbor: "None. Off-grid. No infrastructure to surveil. This is both its danger and its freedom."
    the_spire: "Classified. Assumed total. Nobody gets in to find out."

story_implications: |
  Technology in this world is not a power fantasy. It's a class system.
  The same augment that makes a corporate employee effortlessly competent
  makes a street kid dependent on black-market maintenance. The same
  network that gives a Core resident seamless navigation gives a the Gray Zone
  resident a headache from pop-up ads.

  Kyle's relationship with technology is the story's central metaphor:
  military-grade augments in a body that can no longer afford to maintain
  them. The best hardware in the worst context. A soldier's tools in a
  civilian's life. The body is a contradiction, just like the philosophy.
